stated.value: we already have a fluorescence spectrometer
our only justification is that fluorescence can be very sensitive
we have not identified a fluorescent target, marker or reference relationship
report glucose concentration and viable biomass directly during fermentation

missing: independent laboratory method and values for viable biomass and glucose reference
turbidity or optical density of the broth
probe location, vessel and process conditions

status_reason: The target is defined, but fluorescence cannot measure glucose and no fluorescent target is identified, so the fluorescence concept is blocked and the alternatives depend on missing medium, range and reference facts.
answer: Fluorescence cannot report glucose, because it detects intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is assigned to NIR and Raman. Viable biomass by fluorescence depends on finding a fluorescent marker, and turbidity-based UV-Vis tracks cell density only, so an independent viable-cell laboratory reference is required. Test Raman for glucose first with NIR as the comparison, and screen the broth fluorescence in parallel to decide whether it can contribute to biomass.

inline.headline: Test Raman for glucose in a laboratory fermentation trial, with NIR as the comparison
inline.install: in the fermentation vessel or a sampling loop, location to be confirmed by the client
inline.fiber: Vis-NIR silica fiber (350-2400 nm); Raman excitation 785 nm as in the cited examples, spectral axis in Raman shift (cm-1)
inline.test_against: NIR probe for glucose in the millimolar range
inline.not_final_because: Glucose range, medium, viable-biomass reference and broth turbidity are unknown, and Raman signals are weak and can be masked by fluorescence.

problems.text: Fluorescence is highly sensitive but has low selectivity; it relies on secondary emission of certain substances and most chemicals do not fluoresce, so sensitivity alone does not justify it.
Glucose has no direct fluorescence route in the supplied material: fluorescence targets NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin, while glucose is measured by NIR and Raman.

Viable biomass needs a defined signal and a reference: UV-Vis turbidity correlates with cell density, and no viable-cell measurement is described, so an independent laboratory viability reference is required. NIR combined with fluorescence improved biomass estimates in yeast fermentation.
Fluorescence only works when a fluorescent component is present; no fluorescent target is identified, and the combined-probe work is limited to samples with at least one fluorescent component.

methods.why: Gives direct detection of metabolites such as glucose in aqueous media; the signal is weak and can be masked by fluorescence, so this must be checked in the trial.
Tracks glucose in the millimolar range, but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 percent; suited to online use with fiber probes.
Low-cost real-time biomass monitoring because turbidity correlates with cell density; it does not give viability.
Only useful for biomass if NADH, tryptophan or riboflavin are present and shown in a screen; not a route to glucose.

questions.q: Which organism and medium are used, and is an intrinsic fluorophore such as NADH, tryptophan or riboflavin known to be present?
questions.why: This decides whether the existing fluorescence spectrometer can contribute to biomass at all.

questions.q: What glucose concentration range is expected, and is the broth clear or turbid?
questions.why: NIR works in the millimolar range, and transmission measurements saturate in opaque media.

questions.q: Which independent laboratory methods will provide the viable-biomass and glucose reference values?
questions.why: Turbidity does not measure viability, so a laboratory viability reference is required before any calibration.

experiment.objective: Test whether Raman tracks glucose, and whether any spectral signal tracks viable biomass, against independent laboratory references during fermentation.
steps: Run the existing fluorescence spectrometer on broth samples to check for intrinsic fluorophores (NADH, tryptophan, riboflavin) before any biomass use.
Collect samples over a fermentation run and record Raman and NIR spectra on the same samples.
Measure glucose and viable cell count on the same samples by independent laboratory analysis.
Record UV-Vis turbidity alongside to check its relation to cell density.
Build chemometric models on part of the samples, validate on held-out samples, and compare Raman, NIR and their combination.
experiment.go_no_go: criteria to be set by the client, for example the accuracy the client needs for glucose and for viable biomass

pathway.key_features: No spectral features are given in the enquiry; they must be identified by multivariate analysis of the lab trial spectra.
pathway.path_reason: The lab test must come first, so no solution path can be chosen yet.

multispectral.why: NIR covers major components such as glucose, while fluorescence adds high-sensitivity detection of intrinsic fluorophores; the combination improved biomass in yeast fermentation.
multispectral.test: Compare NIR-only, fluorescence-only and combined models on the same held-out fermentation samples with independent laboratory references; the combination counts only if it beats the best single method.

assumptions: The broth is aqueous and the organism and medium are not stated.
The fluorescence spectrometer's excitation wavelength and detection range are not stated.
Probe placement in the vessel is not stated and is assumed to be possible for an in-process probe.
